title: The agreement that lets separately compiled code work together
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state where any argument and any return value travels, explain why a struct's size changes how it is returned, and name what the ABI covers beyond register assignment.

blocks.text: An Application Binary Interface is the agreement that makes separate compilation possible. Neither side of a call reads the other's source; both follow the same document. This lesson is the System V AMD64 ABI, used by Linux, macOS and the BSDs. Windows x64 is a different agreement, which is why a binary from one does not simply work with the other.

blocks.title: Integer and floating-point arguments are counted separately
blocks.text: A function taking an int, a double, an int and a double does not use four consecutive registers. It uses the first two integer registers and the first two SSE registers, because each class has its own independent sequence. Assuming a single left-to-right ordering is one of the most common mistakes when reading an unfamiliar function signature out of disassembly.

blocks.caption: Verified by compiling exactly that signature
lines: double dmix(int a, double b, int c, double d) { return a*b + c*d; }
cvtsi2sd xmm2, edi        ; a  arrived in edi   (integer class)
cvtsi2sd xmm3, esi        ; c  arrived in esi   (integer class)
mulsd    xmm3, xmm1       ; d  arrived in xmm1  (SSE class)
mulsd    xmm0, xmm2       ; b  arrived in xmm0  (SSE class)
addsd    xmm0, xmm3
ret                       ; the double returns in xmm0
/* Two independent sequences. The integers took the first two integer
registers and the doubles took the first two SSE registers, even though
they alternate in the source. Position in the parameter list does not
determine the register -- position WITHIN ITS CLASS does. */

blocks.text: Returning a structure: three mechanisms, chosen by size

blocks.caption: The same construction at three sizes
lines: struct Small { int a, b; };          /*  8 bytes */
lea ecx, [rdi + 1]
shl rcx, 32
mov eax, edi
or  rax, rcx                     ; BOTH fields packed into rax
ret
struct Med { long a, b; };           /* 16 bytes */
mov rax, rdi                     ; first field in rax
lea rdx, [rdi + 1]               ; second field in rdx
ret
struct Large { long a, b, c, d; };   /* 32 bytes */
mov rax, rdi                     ; rdi is a HIDDEN POINTER to the result
mov qword ptr [rdi], rsi         ; the real argument moved to rsi!
mov qword ptr [rdi + 8], rcx
ret                              ; returns the pointer it was given
/* Three different mechanisms decided purely by size. For the large struct
the caller allocated the space and passed its address as an invisible
first argument, which is why the function's own parameter arrived in rsi
instead of rdi. */

blocks.title: The hidden pointer shifts every other argument
blocks.text: When a returned structure is too large for registers, the caller allocates space and passes its address as an invisible first argument in rdi. Every real parameter then moves one register to the right. Reading such a function and assuming rdi is the first declared parameter gives an answer that is wrong for every argument. The tell is a function that writes through rdi and returns rdi — that pattern almost always means a large structure return.
Variadic functions need one extra thing

blocks.caption: What a call to printf actually looks like
lines: void callprintf(int n, double d) { printf("%d %f\n", n, d); }
mov esi, edi              ; n becomes printf's second argument
lea rdi, [rip + L_.str]   ; the format string becomes the first
mov al, 1                 ; <- AL: how many SSE registers hold arguments
jmp _printf               ## TAILCALL
/* Two things worth noticing. AL must hold the number of vector registers
used when calling a variadic function -- printf reads it to know how many
to save. Forgetting it is a classic crash when calling printf from
hand-written assembly. And the call became a jmp: the compiler tail-called
printf, and even labelled it. */

blocks.text: A variadic function does not know at compile time how many arguments arrived, so it may need to save all the argument registers to memory in order to walk them. Saving the eight SSE registers is expensive and usually unnecessary, so the ABI has the caller put the number actually used in al. Hand-written assembly that calls printf without setting al is a well-known crash, and it is a good illustration that an ABI is a contract with obligations in both directions.

blocks.title: The red zone explains a puzzling absence
blocks.text: A leaf function — one that calls nothing — may use the 128 bytes just below rsp without moving rsp at all, because nothing can overwrite them. So you will see writes to [rsp - 8] in functions that never subtract from rsp. It is a small saving repeated everywhere. Note that it does not exist in kernel code, where an interrupt can use the stack at any moment, which is why kernel builds pass a flag to disable it.
Why two ABIs exist and what it costs

xmm0-xmm3, sharing positions with the integers

blocks.text: Note that rdi and rsi are caller-saved under System V and callee-saved under Windows. This is why the very first thing to establish about an unfamiliar binary is which ABI it follows: read it under the wrong one and every argument is attributed to the wrong parameter, consistently and convincingly.

blocks.expected: Every row of the table confirmed by your own compilation. The 32-byte struct case is the one worth dwelling on: seeing the declared parameter show up in rsi makes the hidden-pointer convention concrete, and it is exactly the situation where misreading a disassembly produces a confident, consistent, wrong answer.

Return: rax (and rdx), or xmm0 (and xmm1) for floating point
Callee-saved: rbx, rbp, r12, r13, r14, r15

checkpoint.prompt: A function is declared f(int a, double b, int c, double d). Where do the four arguments arrive?

choices.A: The first four integer registers, in declaration order
choices.B: All four in xmm0 to xmm3
choices.C: a in edi, b in xmm0, c in xmm1, d in esi
choices.D: a in edi, c in esi, b in xmm0, d in xmm1

checkpoint.explanation: The integer and SSE classes are counted separately. Position within its own class decides the register, not position in the parameter list. Assuming a single left-to-right ordering is a common misreading.

checkpoint.prompt: A function writes four values through rdi and returns rdi. What is it most likely doing?

choices.A: Returning a structure too large for registers
choices.D: Both A and B look identical and cannot be distinguished

checkpoint.explanation: The caller allocated the space and passed its address as a hidden first argument. The tell is that rdi is returned in rax. It also means the function's first declared parameter arrived in rsi, so reading rdi as that parameter would misattribute every argument.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a call to printf set al before the call?

choices.A: It is the format string length
choices.B: It marks the call as variadic to the linker
choices.D: al carries the number of SSE registers holding arguments

checkpoint.explanation: The variadic callee knows how many it must save. Saving all eight SSE registers would usually be wasted work. Hand-written assembly that omits this is a well-known crash when calling printf.

checkpoint.prompt: You see writes to [rsp - 8] in a function that never subtracts from rsp. What is happening?

choices.B: The red zone: a leaf function may use the 128 bytes below rsp without adjusting it, because nothing can overwrite them
choices.C: The write is to the caller's frame

checkpoint.explanation: It saves two instructions in every leaf function. It does not exist in kernel code, where an interrupt could use that stack region at any moment.
